https://www.politico.eu/sponsored-conten.text: This past May and June, while the Strait of Hormuz crisis was at its peak and a fifth of the world’s traded oil was looking for a way around the blockage, researchers from Kapa Research were interviewing the businesses that move the cargo. We spoke with 314 shipowners and C-suite executives ​from​​​ the world’s leading shipping groups and asked them how they see the years ahead. ​ ​​The responses reveal a level of confidence that exceeded expectations. An overwhelming 94​​​ percent​​​​​​​ express optimism about their company’s prospects​, and 70​ percent​​​ believe global shipping is in better shape today than it was five years ago. The Global Shipping Outlook 2026 is Kapa Research’s quantitative study of the industry’s leadership, with respondents across every major shipping region, from Europe’s main maritime cent​er​​​s to the United States and Asia. Because fieldwork ran at the height of the crisis, the survey is a rare real-time record of how shipping leaders think under pressure. Geopolitical crises in Ukraine, the Red Sea and the Middle East are named the most serious problem​s​ for shipping today by 76​ percent​​​ of respondents, the top concern in every region we surveyed. Yet when we asked what the Hormuz crisis means for their own company, 40​ percent​​​ said it creates new opportunities and only 23​ percent​​​ see significant obstacles. ​ ​​Nearly half of the industry’s leadership regards turmoil as good for business​​.​ The logic is pragmatic. Conflict pushes ships onto longer routes, longer routes absorb vessel supply​​ and freight rates rise while demand for goods persists. Shipping moves against the cycle. When instability rises, so do revenues. Advertisement The responses reveal a level of confidence that exceeded expectations. An overwhelming 94​​​ percent​​​​​​​ express optimism about their company’s prospects. ​​The industry also treats this as a lasting reset rather than a temporary challenge. 76​ percent​​​ expect the effects of the Hormuz crisis on global shipping to outlast six months, and opinion splits almost in half on whether this is the sector’s most serious crisis of the past 50 years, ​which covers​​​ the oil shocks, the tanker war, the global financial crisis and C​ovid​​​-19. One phrase from our interviews captures the mindset behind optimism: ​“​​​​Shipping keeps working even when the world stops.​​”​​​​ We therefore asked the uncomfortable question directly. Does global shipping today want peace​​ or does it benefit from turmoil? The peace camp wins, but only just: 54​ percent​​​ to 46​ percent​​​. Even among those who say the crisis hurts their own company, a third concede that the industry gains. Such cando​​r is rare in any sector, and it tempers any expectation that shipping will lobby hard for de-escalation. Markets gaining on volatility do not vote against it. Confidence, however, does not mean that the influence equilibrium stays the same. Asked which power will affect developments in global shipping the most in the years ahead, 76​ percent​​​ of our respondents point to the East, meaning China and India, while 17​ percent​​​ choose the West. China is rated the leading shipbuilding nation by 69​ percent​​​, the operator of the most competitive fleet by 62​ percent​​​ and a near-universal 96​ percent​​​ ​​call its role important for ​​strengthening ​​global shipping. Trust, though, has not moved East with the tonnage. Only 17​ percent​​​ rate Chinese ship management highly, while traditional maritime powers such as Greece, Norway​​ and Germany continue to be recognized as the industry’s superior managers. The same shift appears when executives rate the world’s leaders. Xi Jinping​, the president of China,​ stands alone at the top with a net favourability (percent of positive minus percent of negative views) of ​​+44, ahead of Narendra Modi​, the prime minister of India,​ at +24, while the bottom of the ranking is crowded with political leaders at the cent​er​​​ of today’s wars and confrontations. For an industry that plans in decades, predictability seems to weigh more than political alignment, and maritime leaders reward the global actors who ensure a more predictable environment. Nearly half of the industry’s leadership regards turmoil as good for business​​.​ The study’s technology section shows where the next edge will be decided. Shipping’s digital core has advanced from its experimentation phase. Remote monitoring and voyage optimi​z​​​ation are standard equipment, used by over seven in ten companies, while a second wave, predictive maintenance and ​Internet of Things ​​​sensors, is scaling, and a third, ​artificial intelligence (​AI​)​ analytics and digital twins, is only emerging. Each wave reaches roughly half the companies of the one before it. Tradition survives alongside the sensors, since 70​ percent​​​ still track fleet performance with the noon report (a holdover from the age of sail). ​AI​​​ is the divide to watch​:​​​ 65​ percent​​​ of companies already use or pilot AI, yet only 7​ percent​​​ use it extensively​​ and adoption splits along tonnage lines. Among fleets above one million deadweight ​​tonnes, 79​ percent​​​ work with AI, against 50​ percent​​​ in the mid-sized tier. Scale buys data, teams and budgets, the returns compound, and command of AI and cybersecurity will help set the new shipping hierarchy. As one shipowner told us, “Better positioning produces better data, which produces better positioning.” No such technology will replace shipping crews. The shortage of skilled personnel remains the third most serious problem in the ranking, at 37​ percent​​​, and companies respond with high safety standards, competitive pay, internet access on board and training. Two findings point to a deeper change​:​​​ 72​ percent​​​ of companies intend to employ more women at sea​​ and 74​ percent​​​ now call ESG​ (environment, social, governance)​ performance important to their overall business strategy. Advertisement Shipping keeps working even when the world stops.​ One response from the interviews Shipping carries about four​-​​​fifths of world trade, so the way its leaders think matters far beyond the industry. What they told us at the peak of a crisis is that volatility is now structural, that the cent​er​​​ of maritime gravity is shifting East, and that they plan to keep moving through whatever comes. Governments, corporations and international organi​z​​​ations facing the same instability have lessons to draw from ​their​​​ resilience. ​​The full Global Shipping Outlook 2026 report is available ​ here ​​. ​​A special thanks to LAROS by Prisma Electronics SA for their insights and support in this year’s study.​ The above column is sponsor-generated content. Published by Simon Matthis - 10 Sep, 2026 Nippon Paper Industries Co. has decided today to temporarily suspend the business of Nippon Paper Chemicals Europe Zrt. (“NPCE”), its consolidated subsidiary in Hungary. As a result, the company expects to recognize an extraordinary loss for the expenses associated with the temporary suspension of business. Reasons for the Temporary Suspension of Business In its Medium-Term Business Plan 2030 announced on May 28, 2026, the Company set forth three basic strategies: balance sheet optimization, decisive structural reforms, and profitability improvement. Under these strategies, the Company is working to improve capital efficiency and achieve sustainable growth. NPCE was established in Hungary in 2022 to produce and sell CMC (carboxymethyl cellulose, product name: SUNROSE MAC®) for lithium-ion batteries (“LiBs”) used in electric vehicles (“EV”), and began local production in 2025. However, around the time local production started, the external environment surrounding the EV market has grown increasingly challenging, with successive reviews of environmental regulations by countries in Europe and North America, changes in policies to promote EV adoption, and revisions to subsidy systems. Together with the slowing growth of the EV market in those regions, this has left NPCE facing fiercer competition than ever before on a global scale. The Company has worked to develop new customers for NPCE while strengthening its cost competitiveness. However, with changes in the market environment that were difficult to anticipate, under current conditions, securing stable earnings for the time being is likely to prove difficult, and returns commensurate with the investment can no longer be expected. Accordingly, under the basic strategies set out in the Medium-Term Business Plan 2030, the Company has decided to temporarily suspend the business of NPCE in order to prevent the further losses and deterioration in cash flows that continued operation would entail. The Company will consolidate production of CMC at its Gotsu Mill in Japan and strengthen its competitiveness by improving production efficiency. It will also continue to implement the initiatives set out in the Medium-Term Business Plan 2030, thus enhancing the corporate value of the Nippon Paper Group. https://www.hngn.com/articles/273223/202.text: A Russian jet-powered drone struck the locomotive of a Kyiv-to-Warsaw passenger train at Yahodyn station in western Ukraine on Sunday, about two kilometers from the Polish border, minutes after a diplomatic train carrying former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and security advisers from several European Union states had pulled out of the same station — and while a separate train carrying former CIA Director David Petraeus was still standing at the platform. No one was hurt. Ukraine's state railway said a dispatcher monitoring the airspace detected the drone in time to order an evacuation roughly 15 minutes before impact, and that the diplomatic train had left ahead of schedule because of the threat."It is quite possible that this Russian drone may also have been targeting the diplomatic train," the operator, Ukrzaliznytsia, said in a statement, noting that schedules on the western lines are now adjusted in real time depending on which routes are open and which are under attack. The Western delegation, which included former European leaders, was returning from a conference in Kyiv. Der Spiegel reported that the special train was later halted over a further drone threat and partly evacuated after strikes in the area; among those aboard were Günter Sautter, one of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's closest advisers, and a German Green lawmaker who chairs the Bundestag's Ukraine friendship group. Petraeus, who has traveled to Ukraine repeatedly since 2022 to advise and observe, was on the other train at Yahodyn at the moment the locomotive was hit.Poland's reaction was immediate. "Putin escalates," Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski wrote on social media, and Prime Minister Donald Tusk convened a crisis team for the afternoon. The strike fell within sight of NATO territory on a rail corridor that has become the main civilian and diplomatic artery between Ukraine and the West, and it came at the end of a weekend in which Russia launched 453 drones at Ukraine overnight, hit Odesa for a second consecutive night and struck as far west as Ternopil and Ivano-Frankivsk. Ukrzaliznytsia said the drone was a mesh-network model that navigates by relaying signals between drones, a type Ukraine has increasingly reported over its western regions.The Kremlin, in the same hours, offered a diplomatic signal of a different kind. Spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters that Moscow is open to restarting trilateral talks with Ukraine and the United States as early as October, the first indication of timing since U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Moscow and Kyiv a week ago. Kushner has acknowledged that territory remains the central obstacle. The offer landed on the day President Trump, speaking in Ireland, told Volodymyr Zelensky to stop striking Russian diesel refineries — and on the day a Russian drone came within a few minutes of a train full of European security officials.Whether the locomotive or the delegation was the intended target may never be established; Ukrainian officials did not claim certainty and Moscow did not comment. What the strike established is narrower and, for Warsaw and Berlin, more pointed: Russian drones are now reaching a station two kilometers from Poland on a line that Western governments use to move their own people in and out of Kyiv, and the margin on Sunday was a rescheduled departure and a dispatcher who saw the drone coming.

https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-ukrai.text: BRUSSELS — The European Commission and Ukraine have reached a deal to accelerate the disbursement of €45 billion earmarked for Kyiv in 2027 under the EU’s €90 billion loan program , they said Thursday in a joint statement . Russia has in recent weeks escalated its drone and missile attacks against Ukraine, while the country is running out of funds to buy weapons to defend itself. Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi warned journalists this week that Ukraine faces a $27 billion (€23 billion) defense funding gap this year, with Kyiv hoping to cover about $7 billion domestically and looking to partners for the rest. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that if the gap isn't plugged in the next two months, Kyiv risks being unable to buy weapons early next year. Advertisement Advertisement At a recent meeting of EU defense ministers, "many called for front-loading parts of the €90 billion loan allocated for 2027," meaning disbursing part of the 2027 loan this year instead, the EU's top diplomat Kaja Kallas said last month. But the Commission preferred to instead speed up the disbursement of the 2027 loan next year itself, meaning Ukraine would get that money faster, diplomats said. "Our dialogue with the European Commission has delivered good results in addressing Ukraine's financial and defense needs for 2026 and 2027," Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said . "We have agreed on the format, timeline, and steps needed to ensure full coverage," he added. "For 2027, we have agreed to move forward swiftly with the allocation of €45 billion under the Ukraine Support Loan, subject to the established conditions," the two sides said, referring to the reforms Ukraine must carry out to receive the money. Once Ukraine meets the conditions, the funds will be immediately disbursed, according to a senior EU official. The two sides also agreed that they will "begin work on identifying additional budgetary and defence needs" and meet monthly to coordinate their efforts. The €90 billion EU loan was agreed by leaders last December to provide financial support to Ukraine in 2026 and 2027. It includes strict conditions for Kyiv, including adherence to the rule of law and the fight against corruption. A large share of the loan — €60 billion — is earmarked for Ukraine’s defense needs. Advertisement Advertisement The loan has been split evenly, with €45 billion earmarked for 2026 and another €45 billion for 2027. It was designed to cover two-thirds of Ukraine's external financing needs over the two years, with the rest expected to be covered by other countries, particularly G7 partners. The joint statement also calls on those partners to step in. "All sides agreed that other partners should also fulfil their financial commitments and step up their efforts in light of the significant challenges Ukraine is facing," it says. Zoya Sheftalovich contributed to this report .

https://www.dailysabah.com/politics/blac.text: Politics Diplomacy Legislation War On Terror EU Affairs Elections News Analysis Black Sea drone threats push Türkiye, Romania, Bulgaria toward closer ties by Daily Sabah with AA ISTANBUL Oct 27, 2026 - 11:58 am GMT+3 The cargo ship Royad Mammadov remains half-submerged after being hit by a drone in Romania’s territorial waters, killing two Azerbaijani crew members, Black Sea, Oct. 5, 2026. (Reuters Photo) by Daily Sabah with AA Oct 27, 2026 11:58 am Cooperation between Türkiye, Romania and Bulgaria has become increasingly important for Black Sea security following a surge in drone attacks targeting commercial vessels, with experts calling for stronger regional defense coordination and greater NATO support. Recent attacks on commercial shipping near the Black Sea coasts of Romania and Bulgaria have heightened concerns over maritime safety, highlighting Türkiye's strategic role in securing critical shipping routes and maintaining regional stability. Maria Branea, policy and research coordinator at the European Leadership Network, told Anadolu Agency (AA) that the sharp increase in drone attacks has made a coordinated regional security framework increasingly urgent. "Türkiye is undoubtedly a central actor," Branea said, emphasizing Ankara's naval capabilities and its authority over access to the Black Sea under the Montreux Convention. She also highlighted Türkiye's leadership in negotiating the Black Sea Mine Countermeasures Task Group (MCM Black Sea), describing the initiative as a significant example of regional cooperation. Branea noted that the three NATO allies maintain different strategic priorities. While Türkiye traditionally emphasizes coastal states' leadership and managing tensions with Russia, Romania advocates a stronger NATO presence, and Bulgaria has historically adopted a more cautious approach. Stronger NATO, EU coordination Branea argued that NATO and the European Union should reinforce existing regional initiatives rather than establish new institutions or develop comprehensive strategic frameworks. "In my view, what needs to change is not the creation of a new NATO institution or a comprehensive strategy document," she noted. Instead, she urged both organizations to recognize and strengthen security arrangements already emerging among Türkiye, Romania and Bulgaria. She called for regular consultations among coastal allies, clearer responsibilities, integrated maritime surveillance systems and coordinated investments in defense capabilities. Branea also highlighted the growing importance of protecting offshore energy infrastructure, citing Türkiye's Sakarya gas field and Romania's Neptun Deep project, which is expected to begin production in 2027. She suggested expanding an EU-backed Maritime Security Center proposed by Romania and Bulgaria to include Türkiye, Ukraine and Moldova. Defense cooperation between Türkiye and Ukraine could also be extended to Romania and Bulgaria, supported by sustained investment and closer political and military coordination, according to Branea. Black Sea region has recently been a center of renewed tensions and attacks as part of the Russia-Ukraine conflict, with attacks also weighing on critical trade supplies, including oil and grain exports. Securing maritime routes Dimitar Bechev, a senior fellow at Carnegie Europe, similarly urged Türkiye, Romania and Bulgaria to seek additional NATO assistance and engage Washington on strengthening maritime security. Bechev argued that Russia's primary objective was to weaken European support for Ukraine rather than directly test NATO. He said reviving the original Black Sea Grain Initiative remained unlikely after Russia declined to renew the agreement in 2023. Türkiye, alongside the U.N., was credited with brokering the historic Black Sea Grain Initiative on July 22, 2022, in Istanbul to allow safe maritime passage for Ukrainian agricultural exports during the war with Russia. However, Russia withdrew from the agreement in 2023, complaining that its own ⁠food ​and fertilizer exports faced ​serious obstacles. Instead, he advocated strengthening alternative shipping routes established through the territorial waters of NATO member states. "Navigation through the territorial waters of Romania, Bulgaria and Türkiye must be guaranteed," Bechev underlined, describing secure maritime passage as a minimum requirement.
